analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-discrimination laws to unpaid interns.
analysis.headline: The bill to let unpaid interns sue for workplace discrimination never got a vote, dying in the House Education and Labor Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Unpaid interns currently work without the protections of federal anti-discrimination laws, because those laws cover employees and unpaid interns are not employees. This bill would let interns bring discrimination claims under the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act, and would let them sue states too. The bill was introduced on January 3, 2019, was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Unpaid interns, a population that skews young and includes students earning school credit, would gain the right to sue employers who discriminate against them based on race, sex, national origin, religion, age, or disability.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against an intern based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, or disability, closing a gap in the definition of who counts as an employee [S3].

It applies the same complaint procedures and legal standards already used under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act, so interns would have the same enforcement path as employees [S3] [S2].
Federal courts could award legal and equitable relief to interns who win discrimination claims [S3].
The bill removes states' Eleventh Amendment immunity, so a state agency using unpaid interns could be sued in federal court just like a private employer [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use unpaid interns, including businesses, nonprofits, and state and local governments, would bear the cost of potential lawsuits and discrimination liability.

drawbacks.text: States and employers would face new litigation exposure, and the bill strips the states' usual constitutional immunity from such suits, which defenders of state sovereignty typically oppose [S3].

The bill protects interns from discrimination and harassment but does nothing about the underlying problem that the work itself is unpaid, so it does not improve interns' pay or economic position [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and low-cost: it extends existing legal frameworks to a group that lacks them, rather than creating new obligations. Its main limitation is that it does not address unpaid work itself, only the discrimination interns may face while doing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress, along with original cosponsors Reps. Meng, Scott, and Norton [S1] [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, where it received no further action [S1] [S5].
Only three other members signed on as cosponsors during the two-year Congress, and the bill never came to the House floor [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use unpaid interns, including businesses and governments, avoid discrimination liability that the bill would have created for them.

for.name: Rep. Elijah Cummings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Grace Meng, Bobby Scott, and Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or scheduled it for a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced to a vote where party positions would have been recorded [S4] [S1].

industries.industry: Employers using unpaid interns (businesses, nonprofits, government agencies)
industries.note: The bill would have made these employers subject to discrimination lawsuits by interns, a group they currently do not owe anti-discrimination duties to. The bill's death leaves that liability gap in place.
